name: Inattentional Blindness
statement: Absorbed in one task, people can miss something as obvious as a gorilla in plain sight.
statementAccent: people can miss something as obvious
meaning: Inattentional blindness is the failure to notice a fully visible, often salient, unexpected object or event because attention is engaged elsewhere. When focused on a task, people can miss something obvious right in front of them; the object is registered by the eyes but not consciously perceived, so the failure is one of attention, not eyesight. Its most famous demonstration is the invisible gorilla study by Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris, in which viewers counting basketball passes often fail to see a person in a gorilla suit stroll through the scene. Named by Arien Mack and Irvin Rock, inattentional blindness is a landmark finding in cognitive psychology, showing that attention is necessary for conscious perception and that we see far less of the world than we believe.
mechanism: Perception is not a passive recording of everything in the visual field; conscious awareness requires attention. When attention is fully occupied by a demanding task, an unexpected stimulus, however visible or striking, may never reach conscious perception even though the eyes take it in. In the gorilla experiment, viewers tasked with counting passes among players devote their attention to the ball and the counting, and about half fail to notice the gorilla walking through, facing the camera, and thumping its chest. The heavier the attentional load of the primary task, the more likely the unexpected object is missed. This reveals that seeing, in the sense of conscious awareness, depends on where attention is directed, so much of the visual scene goes unnoticed by default.

examples.text: In Simons and Chabris's 1999 study, about half of viewers counting basketball passes failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walk through the scene.
Drivers absorbed in a task or distracted can miss a motorcycle or pedestrian in plain view, the looked-but-failed-to-see errors implicated in collisions.
Arien Mack and Irvin Rock coined the term inattentional blindness and studied it extensively, culminating in their 1998 book of that name.

variants.name: Change blindness
variants.text: A related but distinct phenomenon, the failure to notice a change to a scene, which requires comparison over time, unlike inattentional blindness's missed unexpected object.

variants.name: The attentional-load factor
variants.text: The finding that the more demanding the primary task, the more likely an unexpected stimulus is missed, tying the effect to how attention is allocated.

whyItMatters: Inattentional blindness is a landmark demonstration that attention is necessary for conscious perception, overturning the intuition that we see everything before our eyes. It has serious real-world implications: distracted drivers miss motorcycles and pedestrians in the looked-but-failed-to-see errors behind many crashes, radiologists can overlook anomalies while focused on a search, and eyewitnesses may miss events unfolding beside them. It informs debates about multitasking, the dangers of phone use while driving, and the reliability of human observation. By revealing how much of the visible world goes unnoticed when attention is elsewhere, it reshapes how we understand vision, awareness, and the limits of the attentive mind.

working.text: accept that when attention is fully engaged, even obvious unexpected objects can go unnoticed, so seeing depends on attending.
in safety-critical tasks like driving, minimise competing demands, since a heavy attentional load makes missing unexpected hazards more likely.
keep inattentional blindness, missing an unexpected object, separate from change blindness, failing to notice a change that requires comparison over time.

limits: Inattentional blindness is a failure of attention and conscious perception, not of the eyes, which register the object, so it is not a defect of eyesight and does not mean the person is careless. It depends on the object being unexpected and attention being engaged elsewhere, so a salient stimulus one is looking for is usually noticed. It is distinct from change blindness, which involves failing to detect a change and requires comparison across time. The proportion who miss the stimulus varies with the task's attentional demands and the observer, so it is a robust tendency rather than a fixed rate, and it reflects normal attention rather than negligence.
misreadings: The missed object is fully visible and registered by the eyes; the failure is attentional and perceptual, not a defect of eyesight, so it is not about seeing poorly. It does not mean the person is careless or negligent; roughly half of ordinary observers miss the gorilla, because this is how attention normally works. And it is distinct from change blindness, which is failing to notice a change and requires comparing two moments, whereas inattentional blindness is failing to notice an unexpected object present all along.
origin: Named and studied extensively by Arien Mack and Irvin Rock, culminating in their 1998 book Inattentional Blindness, and demonstrated dramatically by Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris's 1999 invisible-gorilla study.

sources.text: Inattentional blindness, Wikipedia. — the definition of missing a visible unexpected stimulus, Mack and Rock's term, the Simons and Chabris gorilla study, and driving and other implications.
Simons & Chabris, Gorillas in Our Midst: Sustained Inattentional Blindness for Dynamic Events, Perception (1999). — the invisible-gorilla experiment and the roughly half-miss result.
